reason: The sources provide over a dozen multi-sourced, verified facts detailing Betelgeuse's immense scale, runaway motion, the 2019–2020 Great Dimming, and the dramatic daytime visibility of its eventual supernova.
story: In late 2019, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky began to fade rapidly, fueling worldwide speculation that a cataclysmic stellar explosion was imminent. Betelgeuse, the fiery red shoulder of Orion, plunged to its faintest levels in a century, dropping from the top ten brightest stars down past the top twenty. Betelgeuse is a cosmic titan: wielded at roughly twenty times the Sun's mass, it is bloated enough that if placed in our solar system, it would engulf Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. A runaway star hurtling through space at thirty kilometers per second, it is doomed to end in a brilliant Type II supernova within 100,000 years. When it detonates, it will burn bright enough to be seen in broad daylight and cast nighttime shadows on Earth for months without harming our planet. Ultimately, telescopes proved the 2019 scare wasn't the final blast, but a titanic ejection of gas that cooled into a temporary dust veil.
angle: If Betelgeuse exploded today, it would shine bright enough to cast night shadows on Earth and blaze in broad daylight for months, yet leave our planet completely unharmed.

claims.claim: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star located in the constellation Orion.
If placed at the center of our solar system, Betelgeuse would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Betelgeuse has a mass estimated to be roughly 15 to 20 times that of the Sun.
Betelgeuse is relatively young at around 8.5 to 10 million years old, but is already near the end of its life.
Astronomers estimate that Betelgeuse will end its life in a Type II supernova explosion, likely within the next 100,000 years.
When Betelgeuse explodes as a supernova, it will be bright enough to be visible during the daytime for months.
The supernova explosion will be bright enough at night to rival the moon and cast visible shadows on Earth.
Life on Earth will be completely unharmed when Betelgeuse explodes because it is too far away.
Betelgeuse is a runaway star speeding through the interstellar medium at roughly 30 kilometers per second (about 18.6 miles per second).
As Betelgeuse travels through interstellar space, its stellar wind creates a massive bow shock several light-years wide.
Betelgeuse was ejected from its birthplace in the stellar association that includes the stars in Orion's Belt.
Ancient Chinese astronomers recorded Betelgeuse as a yellow star, while later classical records described it as orange or red, indicating rapid stellar evolution.
The traditional name Betelgeuse is derived from a mistranslation of an Arabic name meaning the hand or armpit of Orion.
Betelgeuse is normally the brightest star in the night sky at infrared wavelengths.
Starting in October 2019, Betelgeuse began dimming dramatically, an event dubbed the Great Dimming.
During the Great Dimming, Betelgeuse fell from among the top 10 brightest stars in the sky to outside the top 20.
The unprecedented fading provoked widespread media and public speculation that Betelgeuse was about to explode.
Hubble Space Telescope observations revealed that Betelgeuse ejected an immense cloud of hot material that cooled into starlight-blocking dust.
By early 2020, Betelgeuse stopped fading and began recovering its normal brightness.
Betelgeuse's brightness regularly varies due to overlapping pulsation cycles, including a ~425-day cycle and a roughly 6-year period.

disputed: Distance to Betelgeuse: Estimates in the sources range from roughly 400 to over 700 light-years (commonly cited around 500–640 ly). The script should state 'roughly 500 to 600 light-years away.'
Bow shock width: Wikipedia and NASA state roughly 4 light-years across, while ESA's Akari team measured it at about 3 light-years. The script should say 'three to four light-years wide.'

Cause of the Great Dimming: Hubble ultraviolet data pointed to a surface mass ejection forming an obscuring dust cloud, while some submillimetre studies suggested giant cool starspots on the photosphere without dust. The script should attribute the dust cloud mechanism to Hubble and ESO observations.

Supernova timeline: Most sources state within the next 100,000 years, while a couple mention up to a million years. The script should state 'expected within the next 100,000 years, according to astronomers.'
